chapter_text:
CHAPTER 6 — PERIODIC CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS

Introduction

By the middle of the nineteenth century chemists had isolated more than sixty elements, each with its own properties. Memorising the properties of every element one by one was impractical. Scientists therefore searched for a way to ORGANISE the elements so that their properties could be understood and predicted from a pattern. This effort to CLASSIFY the elements led, after several attempts, to the Periodic Table — one of the most powerful organising ideas in all of science. This chapter traces that journey: from Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves, through Mendeleev's famous table, to Moseley's atomic-number basis and the Modern Periodic Table we use today, and finally the periodic TRENDS that the table reveals.

6.1 EARLY ATTEMPTS AT CLASSIFICATION

(a) Döbereiner's Triads (1817–1829).
Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner, a German chemist, noticed that certain elements with similar chemical properties could be grouped in sets of THREE called TRIADS. In a triad, the atomic mass of the MIDDLE element was approximately the AVERAGE (arithmetic mean) of the atomic masses of the other two. Classic example — the lithium, sodium, potassium triad: atomic masses 7, 23 and 39. The average of 7 and 39 is (7 + 39) / 2 = 23, which is the atomic mass of sodium. Other triads were calcium–strontium–barium and chlorine–bromine–iodine.
Limitation: only a FEW such triads could be identified among the elements known at the time. Most elements did not fit into any triad, so the scheme was not general.

(b) Newlands' Law of Octaves (1866).
John Newlands, an English chemist, arranged the known elements in order of INCREASING ATOMIC MASS. He found that every EIGHTH element had properties similar to the first — much like the eighth note in a musical octave repeats the first. He called this the LAW OF OCTAVES. For example, starting from lithium: lithium (1), beryllium (2), boron (3), carbon (4), nitrogen (5), oxygen (6), fluorine (7), and the eighth element sodium resembled lithium.
Limitations: (i) The law worked only up to calcium; beyond it the pattern broke down. (ii) It assumed no more elements would be discovered, but many new elements were later found that did not fit. (iii) To make some elements fit, Newlands placed TWO elements in the same slot, and sometimes grouped DISSIMILAR elements together (for example cobalt and nickel with the halogens). The scientific community ridiculed the idea at the time, but Newlands had captured a genuine glimpse of periodicity.

6.2 MENDELEEV'S PERIODIC TABLE (1869)

The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev produced the first widely accepted periodic table. He arranged the 63 elements then known in order of increasing ATOMIC MASS, but — crucially — he grouped together elements with SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES (similar formulae of oxides and hydrides). His guiding statement, MENDELEEV'S PERIODIC LAW, was: 'The properties of elements are a PERIODIC FUNCTION of their atomic masses.' Horizontal rows were PERIODS and vertical columns were GROUPS.

Merits of Mendeleev's table:
 1. GAPS FOR UNDISCOVERED ELEMENTS. Mendeleev had the confidence to leave EMPTY SPACES in his table rather than force a known element into the wrong group. He predicted that elements would later be found to fill these gaps, and he even predicted their properties. He called them eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon ('eka' = Sanskrit for 'one', i.e. 'one place below'). When scandium (eka-boron), gallium (eka-aluminium) and germanium (eka-silicon) were discovered, their measured properties matched Mendeleev's predictions remarkably closely — a triumph that won the table wide acceptance.
 2. CORRECTION OF ATOMIC MASSES. Because he placed elements by properties, Mendeleev was able to correct several wrongly-measured atomic masses (e.g. beryllium, indium, gold).
 3. ACCOMMODATION OF NOBLE GASES. When the noble gases (helium, neon, argon, etc.) were discovered later, they could be added as a new group (zero group) without disturbing the existing arrangement.

Defects (limitations) of Mendeleev's table:
 1. POSITION OF HYDROGEN was not fixed. Hydrogen resembles the alkali metals (group I, forms H⁺) but also resembles the halogens (group VII, forms H⁻ and is diatomic). It could not be assigned a single definite position.
 2. POSITION OF ISOTOPES. Isotopes of an element have DIFFERENT atomic masses but identical chemical properties. On a mass-ordered table they should occupy different positions, yet they are the same element — a contradiction.
 3. ANOMALOUS PAIRS. In a few places a heavier element had to be placed BEFORE a lighter one to keep chemically similar elements together. For example argon (40) was placed before potassium (39), and cobalt (58.9) before nickel (58.7), and tellurium (127.6) before iodine (126.9). Ordering strictly by atomic mass would have put these in the wrong groups.

6.3 MOSELEY AND THE MODERN PERIODIC LAW

In 1913 the English physicist Henry Moseley studied the X-rays emitted by different elements. He found that the frequency of the characteristic X-rays was related not to the atomic mass but to a whole number that increased by one from element to element — the ATOMIC NUMBER (Z), equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Moseley showed that the atomic number, NOT the atomic mass, is the truly fundamental property of an element. Ordering elements by atomic number automatically removed the anomalous pairs of Mendeleev's table (argon Z = 18 naturally comes before potassium Z = 19; cobalt Z = 27 before nickel Z = 28; tellurium Z = 52 before iodine Z = 53) and explained why isotopes occupy the same place (they have the same Z).

This led to the MODERN PERIODIC LAW: 'The properties of elements are a PERIODIC FUNCTION of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.' Because elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, and the chemistry of an atom is governed by its electron arrangement, atomic number (which fixes the electron configuration) is the natural basis for the table.

6.4 STRUCTURE OF THE MODERN PERIODIC TABLE

The modern (long-form) periodic table arranges all the known elements in order of increasing atomic number. It has:
 • 7 horizontal rows called PERIODS (numbered 1 to 7). The period number equals the number of OCCUPIED electron shells in the atoms of that period. Period 1 has only 2 elements (H, He); periods 2 and 3 have 8 each; periods 4 and 5 have 18 each; periods 6 and 7 have 32 each (including the lanthanides and actinides shown separately below the main table).
 • 18 vertical columns called GROUPS (numbered 1 to 18). Elements in the same group have the SAME number of VALENCE ELECTRONS, so they show similar chemical properties. Important groups: group 1 = alkali metals; group 2 = alkaline earth metals; group 17 = halogens; group 18 = noble gases.
 • BLOCKS based on the sub-shell being filled: the s-block (groups 1–2), the p-block (groups 13–18), the d-block or transition metals (groups 3–12), and the f-block (lanthanides and actinides) placed below the table.

The position of an element — its period and group — can be read directly from its electronic configuration: the period number = the highest shell number occupied; the group (for s- and p-block elements) is related to the number of valence electrons.

6.5 PERIODIC PROPERTIES (TRENDS)

Because properties repeat periodically, definite TRENDS appear as we move across a period or down a group.

(a) ATOMIC SIZE (atomic radius) — the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell.
 • ACROSS A PERIOD (left to right): atomic size DECREASES. Electrons are being added to the SAME shell while the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases. The greater pull of the nucleus draws the electron cloud inward, so the atom gets smaller.
 • DOWN A GROUP (top to bottom): atomic size INCREASES. Each successive element has one MORE electron shell, so the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus despite the increased nuclear charge.

(b) METALLIC AND NON-METALLIC CHARACTER.
 Metallic character = the tendency to LOSE electrons (electropositive character). Non-metallic character = the tendency to GAIN electrons.
 • ACROSS A PERIOD: metallic character DECREASES and non-metallic character INCREASES (the left side is metals, the right side non-metals).
 • DOWN A GROUP: metallic character INCREASES and non-metallic character DECREASES (larger atoms lose electrons more easily).

(c) VALENCY.
 • ACROSS A PERIOD: valency first INCREASES from 1 to 4 and then DECREASES to 0 (for the noble gas). It is governed by the number of valence electrons (valency = number of valence electrons, or 8 minus that number).
 • DOWN A GROUP: valency remains the SAME, because all members of a group have the same number of valence electrons.

(d) ELECTRONEGATIVITY — the tendency of an atom to ATTRACT the shared pair of electrons in a bond.
 • ACROSS A PERIOD: electronegativity INCREASES (smaller atoms with higher nuclear charge attract electrons more strongly). Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
 • DOWN A GROUP: electronegativity DECREASES (the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so the atom attracts bonding electrons less strongly).

SUMMARY

- Döbereiner grouped similar elements in TRIADS where the middle atomic mass is the average of the other two; only a few triads existed.
- Newlands' LAW OF OCTAVES said every eighth element repeats properties; it worked only up to calcium.
- Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and grouped them by properties; his PERIODIC LAW made properties a periodic function of atomic mass. He left GAPS and predicted eka-boron (Sc), eka-aluminium (Ga) and eka-silicon (Ge). Defects: position of hydrogen, isotopes, and anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I).
- Moseley showed ATOMIC NUMBER, not atomic mass, is fundamental. The MODERN PERIODIC LAW: properties are a periodic function of atomic number. This removed the anomalies and explained isotopes.
- The Modern Periodic Table has 7 PERIODS and 18 GROUPS, divided into s-, p-, d- and f-blocks. Period number = number of shells; group members share the same number of valence electrons.
- Trends: across a period atomic size decreases, metallic character decreases, non-metallic character and electronegativity increase. Down a group atomic size and metallic character increase, electronegativity decreases, valency stays the same.

topics.description: The long-form table: 7 periods and 18 groups; s-, p-, d- and f-blocks; period number = number of shells; group members share the same number of valence electrons; alkali metals, halogens and noble gases.

topics.description: How atomic size, metallic/non-metallic character, valency and electronegativity vary across a period from left to right, and the reasons (increasing nuclear charge within the same shell).

topics.description: How atomic size, metallic/non-metallic character, valency and electronegativity vary down a group from top to bottom, and the reasons (addition of new shells).

chapter_summary.title: Periodic Classification of Elements — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 6. It traces the development of the periodic table from Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves, through Mendeleev's atomic-mass table (with its predictions and defects), to Moseley's atomic-number basis and the Modern Periodic Law. It then describes the structure of the Modern Periodic Table (7 periods, 18 groups, s/p/d/f blocks) and the periodic trends across periods and down groups.

sections.heading: Early attempts at classification
bullets: Döbereiner (1817–1829) grouped chemically similar elements into TRIADS in which the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two — e.g. Li(7), Na(23), K(39), with (7+39)/2 = 23.
Only a few triads (Li-Na-K, Ca-Sr-Ba, Cl-Br-I) could be found, so the scheme was not general.
Newlands (1866) arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found every EIGHTH element had similar properties — the LAW OF OCTAVES, by analogy with musical notes.
Newlands' law worked only up to calcium, assumed no new elements would be found, and forced dissimilar elements together — so it was eventually rejected.

sections.heading: Mendeleev's periodic table
bullets: Mendeleev (1869) arranged the 63 known elements by increasing atomic mass but grouped them by similar chemical properties into PERIODS (rows) and GROUPS (columns).
His PERIODIC LAW: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
He left GAPS for undiscovered elements and predicted the properties of eka-boron (scandium), eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium) — later confirmed.
Defects: no fixed position for hydrogen; isotopes (same element, different mass) could not be placed; a few anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) needed a heavier element before a lighter one.

sections.heading: Moseley and the Modern Periodic Law
bullets: Moseley (1913) studied the X-ray spectra of elements and showed that the ATOMIC NUMBER (number of protons), not the atomic mass, is the fundamental property of an element.
The MODERN PERIODIC LAW states: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.
Ordering by atomic number removes Mendeleev's anomalous pairs (Ar before K, Co before Ni, Te before I) and explains why isotopes share the same position (same Z).

sections.heading: Structure of the Modern Periodic Table
bullets: There are 7 PERIODS (horizontal rows); the period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in the atom.
There are 18 GROUPS (vertical columns); elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and hence similar chemical properties.
The table is divided into s-block (groups 1–2), p-block (groups 13–18), d-block / transition metals (groups 3–12) and f-block (lanthanides and actinides).
Group 1 = alkali metals, group 2 = alkaline earth metals, group 17 = halogens, group 18 = noble gases.

sections.heading: Periodic trends across periods and down groups
bullets: ATOMIC SIZE decreases across a period (rising nuclear charge in the same shell) and increases down a group (new shells added).
METALLIC character decreases and NON-METALLIC character increases across a period; metallic character increases down a group.
VALENCY rises from 1 to 4 then falls to 0 across a period, but stays the same down a group.
ELECTRONEGATIVITY increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.

key_takeaways: Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves were early glimpses of periodicity but worked only for a few elements.
Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass, grouped them by properties, and famously left gaps to predict eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon.
Mendeleev's defects were the position of hydrogen, the placement of isotopes, and the anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I).
Moseley showed that ATOMIC NUMBER is the fundamental property, giving the Modern Periodic Law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
The Modern Periodic Table has 7 periods (= number of shells) and 18 groups (= same valence electrons), divided into s-, p-, d- and f-blocks.
Across a period: atomic size decreases, metallic character decreases, electronegativity and non-metallic character increase.
Down a group: atomic size and metallic character increase, electronegativity decreases, and valency stays the same.

glossary.definition: A group of three chemically similar elements in which the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the average of the masses of the other two (e.g. Li, Na, K).
Newlands' rule that when elements are arranged by increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first, like notes in a musical octave.
The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
A horizontal row in the periodic table; the period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in the atoms of that row.
A vertical column in the periodic table; elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.
Mendeleev's name for a predicted, yet-undiscovered element placed one position below a known one (e.g. eka-silicon = germanium).
A pair such as Ar/K, Co/Ni or Te/I where a heavier element had to be placed before a lighter one in Mendeleev's mass-ordered table to keep similar elements together.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; the fundamental property on which the modern periodic table is based.
The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost electron shell of an atom; decreases across a period and increases down a group.
The tendency of an atom to lose electrons (electropositive character); decreases across a period and increases down a group.
The tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons in a chemical bond; increases across a period and decreases down a group.
The combining capacity of an element, set by its valence electrons; across a period it rises from 1 to 4 then falls to 0, and it stays constant down a group.
The very reactive non-metals of group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I, At), each with 7 valence electrons and valency 1.
The unreactive elements of group 18 (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) with complete outer shells and valency 0.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Periodic Classification of Elements (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-6 for Lesson 6. Attempt all questions. Refer to the periodic table for atomic numbers and atomic masses where needed.

questions.question: Verify whether lithium (7), sodium (23) and potassium (39) form a Döbereiner triad. Show the calculation.
questions.answer:
A Döbereiner triad is a group of three chemically similar elements in which the atomic mass of the MIDDLE element is approximately the AVERAGE of the masses of the other two.
Here the three alkali metals are Li (mass 7), Na (mass 23) and K (mass 39).
Average of the first and third = (7 + 39) / 2 = 46 / 2 = 23.
This equals the atomic mass of the middle element, sodium (23).
Therefore Li, Na, K DO form a Döbereiner triad.
questions.explanation: Apply the triad rule: middle mass = average of the other two.

questions.question: State Newlands' law of octaves and give two of its limitations.
questions.answer:
Newlands' LAW OF OCTAVES: when the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, every EIGHTH element has properties similar to the first — just as the eighth note of a musical scale resembles the first.
Two limitations:
 1. The law was valid only up to CALCIUM; beyond it the pattern broke down.
 2. It assumed that no new elements would be discovered, but later discoveries did not fit; to make elements fit, Newlands sometimes placed two elements in one slot or grouped dissimilar elements together.

questions.question: State Mendeleev's periodic law. On what basis did he arrange the elements?
questions.answer:
MENDELEEV'S PERIODIC LAW: 'The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.'
Basis of arrangement: Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of INCREASING ATOMIC MASS, but he grouped together elements having SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES (similar formulae of their oxides and hydrides). The horizontal rows are PERIODS and the vertical columns are GROUPS. Where a known element did not fit a group, he left a GAP rather than force it into the wrong place.
questions.explanation: Periodic law statement plus the mass-with-similar-properties basis.

questions.question: Describe two merits and two defects of Mendeleev's periodic table.
questions.answer:
MERITS:
 1. PREDICTION OF UNDISCOVERED ELEMENTS. Mendeleev left GAPS in his table and predicted the properties of the elements that would fill them — eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. When scandium, gallium and germanium were later discovered, their properties closely matched his predictions, which strongly validated the table.
 2. CORRECTION OF ATOMIC MASSES AND ROOM FOR NOBLE GASES. By placing elements according to properties, he corrected several wrongly measured atomic masses (e.g. beryllium, gold). Later, the newly discovered noble gases were accommodated as a separate group without disturbing the rest of the table.

DEFECTS:
 1. POSITION OF HYDROGEN. Hydrogen resembles both the alkali metals (group I, forms H⁺) and the halogens (group VII, diatomic, forms H⁻), so it could not be given a single fixed position.
 2. ISOTOPES AND ANOMALOUS PAIRS. Isotopes of an element have different atomic masses but the same chemistry, so a mass-ordered table could not place them sensibly. Also, in a few anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) a heavier element had to be placed before a lighter one to keep chemically similar elements together.
questions.explanation: Two merits (predictions/gaps, corrections/noble gases) and two defects (hydrogen, isotopes/anomalous pairs).

questions.question: What was Moseley's contribution, and what is the Modern Periodic Law?
questions.answer:
Henry Moseley (1913) studied the characteristic X-rays emitted by elements and showed that their frequency depends on a whole number that increases by one from element to element — the ATOMIC NUMBER (number of protons). He concluded that the atomic NUMBER, not the atomic MASS, is the fundamental property of an element.
This gave the MODERN PERIODIC LAW: 'The properties of elements are a periodic function of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.' Ordering by atomic number removed Mendeleev's anomalous pairs and explained why isotopes occupy the same position.
questions.explanation: Moseley = atomic number fundamental; modern law statement.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the Modern Periodic Table: periods, groups and blocks.
questions.answer:
The Modern (long-form) Periodic Table arranges all elements in order of increasing ATOMIC NUMBER.
PERIODS: there are 7 horizontal rows called periods. The period number equals the number of OCCUPIED electron shells. Period 1 has 2 elements, periods 2 and 3 have 8 each, periods 4 and 5 have 18 each, and periods 6 and 7 have 32 each (the lanthanides and actinides are shown separately below).
GROUPS: there are 18 vertical columns called groups. Elements in the same group have the SAME number of VALENCE ELECTRONS and therefore similar chemical properties. Group 1 = alkali metals, group 2 = alkaline earth metals, group 17 = halogens, group 18 = noble gases.
BLOCKS: based on the sub-shell being filled — the s-block (groups 1–2), the p-block (groups 13–18), the d-block or transition metals (groups 3–12) and the f-block (lanthanides and actinides) placed below the main table.
An element's position follows from its electronic configuration: the period number = the highest occupied shell, and for s- and p-block elements the group is fixed by the number of valence electrons.
questions.explanation: 7 periods (= shells), 18 groups (= valence electrons), s/p/d/f blocks.

questions.question: How does atomic size vary (a) across a period and (b) down a group? Give reasons.
questions.answer:
(a) ACROSS A PERIOD (left to right): atomic size DECREASES. Electrons are added to the SAME outermost shell while the nuclear charge (protons) increases, so the stronger nuclear pull draws the electron cloud closer and the atom becomes smaller.
(b) DOWN A GROUP (top to bottom): atomic size INCREASES. Each successive element has one MORE electron shell, so the outermost electrons lie farther from the nucleus; this outweighs the increased nuclear charge, and the atom becomes larger.
questions.explanation: Across: decreases (same shell, more charge). Down: increases (new shells).

questions.question: How do metallic character and electronegativity change down a group? Explain.
questions.answer:
DOWN A GROUP (top to bottom):
 • METALLIC character INCREASES. Atoms get larger (new shells are added) and the outer electrons are held less tightly, so they are LOST more easily — the defining behaviour of a metal.
 • ELECTRONEGATIVITY DECREASES. Because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, the atom attracts a shared (bonding) electron pair less strongly.
So as we go down a group, elements become more metallic and less electronegative.
questions.explanation: Down a group: metallic up (bigger atoms lose e easily); electronegativity down (outer e farther/shielded).

questions.question: Why was argon (atomic mass 40) placed before potassium (atomic mass 39) in the modern table even though argon is heavier?
questions.answer:
In Mendeleev's mass-ordered table this Ar/K case was an ANOMALOUS PAIR: ordering strictly by atomic mass would place argon (40) after potassium (39), but their chemistry demands the opposite — argon is an unreactive noble gas and potassium is a reactive alkali metal.
The Modern Periodic Table is ordered by ATOMIC NUMBER, not atomic mass. Argon has Z = 18 and potassium has Z = 19, so argon NATURALLY comes before potassium. Moseley's atomic-number basis therefore resolves the anomaly automatically and places each element in its correct group.
questions.explanation: Atomic-number ordering (Ar 18 before K 19) resolves the mass anomaly.

questions.question: An element X has electronic configuration 2, 8, 7. Predict its period, group type and valency.
questions.answer:
Configuration 2, 8, 7 has THREE occupied shells, so the element lies in PERIOD 3.
Its outermost shell has 7 valence electrons, which places it among the HALOGENS (group 17) — a non-metal. This element is chlorine (Z = 2+8+7 = 17).
Valency: 7 valence electrons is more than 4, so valency = 8 − 7 = 1.
So X is in period 3, group 17 (a halogen), with valency 1.
questions.explanation: 3 shells -> period 3; 7 valence e -> group 17 halogen; valency 8-7 = 1.

A group of three elements with related atomic masses is called a ____.

questions.explanation: Bigger atoms lose electrons more easily.

questions.question: What is a Döbereiner triad? Give one example.
questions.answer: A Döbereiner triad is a group of THREE chemically similar elements arranged so that the atomic mass of the MIDDLE element is approximately the AVERAGE of the atomic masses of the other two. Example: lithium (7), sodium (23) and potassium (39), where (7 + 39)/2 = 23 = mass of sodium. Other examples are Ca-Sr-Ba and Cl-Br-I.

questions.question: Check whether Ca(40), Sr(88) and Ba(137) form a triad.
questions.answer: Average of the first and third masses = (40 + 137)/2 = 177/2 = 88.5. The atomic mass of the middle element, strontium, is about 88, which is very close to 88.5. Since the middle mass is approximately the average of the other two, Ca, Sr, Ba DO form a Döbereiner triad.

questions.question: Why was Döbereiner's triad scheme not accepted as a general classification?
questions.answer: Because only a FEW triads could be found among the elements known at the time (such as Li-Na-K, Ca-Sr-Ba and Cl-Br-I). The majority of elements did not fit into any triad, so the scheme could not classify all the elements. A useful classification must apply to every element, not just a handful, so the triad idea remained only a partial insight.
questions.explanation: Only a few triads -> not general.

questions.question: State Newlands' law of octaves.
questions.answer: Newlands' LAW OF OCTAVES states that when the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, every EIGHTH element has properties similar to the first — just as the eighth note in a musical octave resembles the first note.

questions.question: Give two reasons why Newlands' law of octaves was rejected.
questions.answer:
(1) It was valid only up to CALCIUM; beyond calcium, every eighth element no longer resembled the first.
(2) It assumed that all elements had already been discovered and that no new ones would appear. When new elements were later found, they did not fit the octave pattern, and to force a fit Newlands sometimes placed two elements in one position or grouped dissimilar elements (e.g. cobalt/nickel with halogens) together.
questions.explanation: Limited to Ca; assumed no new elements / forced fits.

questions.question: How was Newlands' work both right and wrong?
questions.answer:
RIGHT: Newlands correctly recognised that the properties of elements REPEAT at regular intervals when arranged by atomic mass — a real glimpse of PERIODICITY, which is the central idea of the modern table.
WRONG: He made the periodicity too rigid (exactly every eighth element) and assumed no new elements would be found. The law broke down beyond calcium and forced dissimilar elements together, so it could not serve as a general classification.
questions.explanation: Captured periodicity but applied it too rigidly.

questions.question: State Mendeleev's periodic law.
questions.answer: MENDELEEV'S PERIODIC LAW: 'The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.' This means that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals.

questions.question: On what TWO criteria did Mendeleev arrange the elements?
questions.answer:
(1) ATOMIC MASS: elements were placed in order of increasing atomic mass.
(2) SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES: elements with similar properties — especially similar formulae of their oxides and hydrides — were placed together in the same vertical column (group). Where these two criteria conflicted, Mendeleev gave priority to chemical properties, even leaving GAPS or reversing a pair when necessary.

questions.question: What are periods and groups in Mendeleev's table?
questions.answer: PERIODS are the HORIZONTAL ROWS of the periodic table. GROUPS are the VERTICAL COLUMNS. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties; moving along a period, properties change gradually from one element to the next.

questions.question: Explain how Mendeleev's gaps led to the discovery of new elements.
questions.answer: Rather than force a known element into the wrong group, Mendeleev left EMPTY SPACES (gaps) in his table wherever a suitable element had not yet been discovered. For each gap he PREDICTED the properties (atomic mass, density, oxide formula, etc.) of the missing element, naming them eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. Chemists then searched for elements with those exact properties. When scandium, gallium and germanium were discovered, their measured properties matched Mendeleev's predictions closely — confirming both the elements and the validity of his table.
questions.explanation: Predicted gap properties guided successful searches.

questions.question: Why was the position of hydrogen a defect in Mendeleev's table?
questions.answer: Hydrogen shows a DUAL nature. Like the alkali metals (group I), it has one valence electron, forms H⁺ ions and a chloride HCl. But like the halogens (group VII), it is diatomic (H₂), can gain an electron to form H⁻ (as in hydrides like NaH), and is a non-metallic gas. Since it resembles BOTH groups, hydrogen could not be assigned a single, definite position — this was a clear defect of the table.
questions.explanation: H resembles both group I and group VII.

questions.question: Explain the anomalous-pairs defect of Mendeleev's table with an example.
questions.answer:
In a strictly mass-ordered table, some adjacent elements would fall into the WRONG groups based on their chemistry. To keep chemically similar elements together, Mendeleev had to place a HEAVIER element BEFORE a lighter one — an 'anomalous pair'.
Example: argon (atomic mass 40) was placed BEFORE potassium (atomic mass 39), even though argon is heavier, because argon is an unreactive gas (belonging with the noble gases) and potassium is a reactive alkali metal. Other anomalous pairs are cobalt/nickel and tellurium/iodine. These reversals violated his own atomic-mass rule and were a recognised defect, later resolved by ordering with atomic number.
questions.explanation: Ar before K (and Co/Ni, Te/I) break the mass rule.

questions.question: Was Mendeleev's decision to leave gaps a strength or a weakness? Justify.
questions.answer: It was a clear STRENGTH. By leaving gaps instead of forcing known elements into unsuitable places, Mendeleev kept each group chemically consistent and made his table PREDICTIVE rather than merely descriptive. The predicted properties of eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon were later confirmed by the discovery of scandium, gallium and germanium. This predictive success is precisely what raised his table above earlier schemes and won it wide acceptance — so leaving gaps was one of its greatest strengths.
questions.explanation: Strength: gaps made the table predictive and were confirmed.

questions.question: What did Moseley discover about the elements?
questions.answer: Henry Moseley (1913), by measuring the frequencies of the characteristic X-rays emitted by different elements, discovered that these frequencies depend on a whole number that increases by exactly ONE from element to element — the ATOMIC NUMBER (the number of protons). He concluded that the atomic NUMBER, not the atomic MASS, is the fundamental property that determines an element's properties.

questions.question: State the Modern Periodic Law and how it differs from Mendeleev's law.
questions.answer:
MODERN PERIODIC LAW: 'The properties of elements are a periodic function of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.'
Difference: Mendeleev's law made properties a periodic function of ATOMIC MASS, whereas the modern law uses ATOMIC NUMBER. The change from mass to number (following Moseley) removed the anomalous pairs and explained the placement of isotopes, making the table internally consistent.
questions.explanation: Modern = function of atomic number, not mass.

questions.question: How does atomic-number ordering remove Mendeleev's anomalous pairs?
questions.answer: Mendeleev's anomalies (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) arose because, although the heavier element belonged chemically AFTER the lighter one, its atomic MASS was higher. In the modern table elements are ordered by ATOMIC NUMBER, which increases by one without exception. Argon (Z = 18) automatically precedes potassium (Z = 19); cobalt (Z = 27) precedes nickel (Z = 28); tellurium (Z = 52) precedes iodine (Z = 53). The chemically correct order and the numerical order now AGREE, so the anomalies disappear.
questions.explanation: Z increases regularly, putting each element in its correct place.

questions.question: Why do isotopes not cause a problem in the modern table?
questions.answer: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons (same ATOMIC NUMBER) but different numbers of neutrons (different atomic masses). Because the modern table is arranged by atomic number, all isotopes of an element share the SAME atomic number and therefore occupy the SAME position. In Mendeleev's mass-ordered table they would have had to go in different places, which was a defect; atomic-number ordering resolves it.

questions.question: How many periods and groups are there in the Modern Periodic Table?
questions.answer: The Modern Periodic Table has 7 PERIODS (horizontal rows) and 18 GROUPS (vertical columns).

questions.question: What do the period number and the group tell us about an atom?
questions.answer: The PERIOD NUMBER equals the number of OCCUPIED electron shells in the atom — so it tells how many shells the atom has. The GROUP (for s- and p-block elements) tells the number of VALENCE ELECTRONS in the outermost shell, which determines the element's chemical behaviour. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and hence similar properties.

questions.question: Name the four blocks of the periodic table and the groups in each.
questions.answer:
s-BLOCK: groups 1 and 2 (the outer s sub-shell is filling).
p-BLOCK: groups 13 to 18 (the outer p sub-shell is filling).
d-BLOCK (transition metals): groups 3 to 12 (the d sub-shell is filling).
f-BLOCK (lanthanides and actinides): shown separately below the main table (the f sub-shell is filling).

questions.question: An element has electronic configuration 2, 8, 8, 1. Find its period and group.
questions.answer: The configuration 2, 8, 8, 1 has FOUR occupied shells, so the element is in PERIOD 4. Its outermost shell has 1 valence electron, so it belongs to GROUP 1 (the alkali metals). The element is potassium (Z = 2+8+8+1 = 19).

questions.question: How does atomic size change across a period and why?
questions.answer: Across a period, from left to right, atomic size DECREASES. As we move along the period, electrons are added to the SAME outermost shell while the number of protons (nuclear charge) increases. The greater nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud more strongly toward the nucleus, so the atom becomes smaller.
questions.explanation: Decreases: same shell, more nuclear charge.

questions.question: Why does metallic character decrease across a period?
questions.answer: Metallic character is the tendency of an atom to LOSE electrons. Across a period the nuclear charge increases and the atomic size decreases, so the outer electrons are held MORE tightly. This makes it harder to remove them, so the elements lose their metallic (electron-donating) character and become more non-metallic (electron-accepting) toward the right side of the period.
questions.explanation: Tighter hold on electrons -> harder to lose -> less metallic.

questions.question: Arrange Na, Mg, Al, Si in order of decreasing atomic size and explain.
questions.answer:
Order of DECREASING size: Na > Mg > Al > Si.
All four are in period 3, so they have the same number of shells, but the nuclear charge rises from Na (11) to Mg (12) to Al (13) to Si (14). The greater the nuclear charge, the more tightly the same outer shell is pulled in, so the atom gets smaller from left to right. Hence sodium is the largest and silicon the smallest.
questions.explanation: Na largest, Si smallest; size falls as Z rises across the period.

questions.question: Why does electronegativity increase across a period?
questions.answer: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to ATTRACT the shared (bonding) electron pair. Across a period the nuclear charge increases and the atomic size decreases, so the nucleus exerts a STRONGER pull on the bonding electrons. Therefore electronegativity increases from left to right, reaching a maximum at the halogens (fluorine being the most electronegative element). Noble gases are usually excluded as they rarely form bonds.
questions.explanation: Higher charge + smaller size -> stronger pull on bonding electrons.

questions.question: How does atomic size change down a group and why?
questions.answer: Down a group, from top to bottom, atomic size INCREASES. Each successive element has one MORE electron shell than the one above it, so the outermost electrons lie progressively farther from the nucleus. Although the nuclear charge also increases, the addition of new shells (and the shielding by inner electrons) dominates, so the atom gets larger.
questions.explanation: Increases: a new shell is added at each step.

questions.question: Why does metallic character increase down a group?
questions.answer: Metallic character is the tendency to LOSE electrons. Down a group, atomic size increases as new shells are added, so the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells. They are therefore held less tightly and are LOST more easily. Because losing electrons is the defining behaviour of a metal, metallic character (reactivity of metals) increases down the group.
questions.explanation: Bigger, more shielded atoms lose outer electrons more easily.

questions.question: Why do all the elements of group 1 have the same valency?
questions.answer: All group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) have exactly ONE valence electron in their outermost shell. Valency is determined by the number of valence electrons, and since each of these atoms loses its single outer electron to achieve a stable noble-gas configuration, each has a valency of 1. Because the number of valence electrons is the same for the whole group, the valency stays the same down the group, even though atomic size and reactivity change.
questions.explanation: Same number of valence electrons (1) -> same valency.

questions.question: Among Li, Na and K, which loses its valence electron most easily? Explain.
questions.answer: POTASSIUM (K) loses its valence electron most easily. Going down group 1 from Li to Na to K, the atomic size increases because new shells are added, so the single outermost electron in potassium is the farthest from the nucleus and the most shielded. Being held least tightly, it is removed most easily. This is why metallic character and reactivity increase down the group: K is more reactive than Na, which is more reactive than Li.
questions.explanation: K largest -> outer electron least tightly held -> lost most easily.

questions.question: 'Fluorine is more reactive as a non-metal than iodine.' Justify using group trends.
questions.answer: Both fluorine and iodine are in group 17 (halogens), which react by GAINING one electron. Non-metallic reactivity depends on how strongly an atom attracts an extra electron — i.e. on its electronegativity and small size. Down the group from F to Cl to Br to I, atomic size INCREASES and electronegativity DECREASES, because the incoming electron is added to a shell farther from the nucleus and more shielded. Fluorine, being the smallest and most electronegative, attracts an electron most strongly and is the most reactive non-metal; iodine, being larger and less electronegative, attracts an electron least strongly and is the least reactive of the four. Hence fluorine is more reactive as a non-metal than iodine.
questions.explanation: F smallest/most electronegative -> attracts electron strongest -> most reactive non-metal.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the early 1800s Döbereiner noticed that some elements could be grouped in threes. In each such group, when the elements were arranged by increasing atomic mass, the middle element's mass was close to the average of the other two. One example is the group lithium (7), sodium (23), potassium (39).

(i) What name is given to such a group of three elements?
(ii) Verify the relationship for Li, Na, K.
(iii) Name one other triad.
(iv) State the main limitation of this scheme.
questions.answer:
(i) A Döbereiner TRIAD.
(ii) Average of the first and third masses = (7 + 39)/2 = 46/2 = 23, which equals the atomic mass of the middle element sodium. So the relationship holds.
(iii) Another triad is chlorine–bromine–iodine (Cl, Br, I) or calcium–strontium–barium (Ca, Sr, Ba).
(iv) The main limitation is that only a FEW triads could be identified; most elements did not fit into any triad, so the scheme was not a general classification.
questions.explanation: Identify triad, verify average, give another, state limitation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Newlands arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and found that every eighth element resembled the first, like notes in a musical scale. He called this the law of octaves.

(i) On what property did Newlands base his arrangement?
(ii) State the law of octaves.
(iii) Up to which element was the law valid?
(iv) Give one reason the law was eventually rejected.
questions.answer:
(i) On increasing ATOMIC MASS.
(ii) Law of octaves: when elements are arranged by increasing atomic mass, every EIGHTH element has properties similar to the first.
(iii) The law was valid only up to CALCIUM.
(iv) It assumed no new elements would be discovered, but later-found elements did not fit; to force fits, Newlands grouped dissimilar elements together (e.g. cobalt/nickel with halogens), so the law broke down.
questions.explanation: Mass basis, statement, valid up to Ca, reason for rejection.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1869 Mendeleev arranged 63 elements in order of increasing atomic mass and grouped together those with similar chemical properties. He summarised his arrangement in a periodic law.

(i) State Mendeleev's periodic law.
(ii) What are the rows and columns of his table called?
(iii) Apart from atomic mass, what did he use to decide an element's group?
(iv) Roughly how many elements were known when he made his table?
questions.answer:
(i) Mendeleev's periodic law: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
(ii) Rows are PERIODS and columns are GROUPS.
(iii) He used the SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES of elements (similar formulae of oxides and hydrides) to decide their group.
(iv) About 63 elements were known at the time.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Mendeleev's table had remarkable successes but also clear defects. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, yet certain elements and pairs did not fit neatly.

(i) Name the three elements Mendeleev predicted and what they later turned out to be.
(ii) Why could hydrogen not be placed definitely?
(iii) Give one anomalous pair and explain the problem.
(iv) Why were isotopes a problem for his table?
questions.answer:
(i) eka-boron = scandium, eka-aluminium = gallium, eka-silicon = germanium.
(ii) Hydrogen resembles BOTH the alkali metals (one valence electron, forms H⁺) and the halogens (diatomic, forms H⁻), so it could not be given one fixed position.
(iii) Anomalous pair: argon (mass 40) had to be placed BEFORE potassium (mass 39), even though argon is heavier, so that each fell in its correct group. This violated the atomic-mass ordering. (Co/Ni and Te/I are similar cases.)
(iv) Isotopes of an element have different atomic masses but identical chemistry. A table ordered by mass would place them at different positions, although they are the same element — a contradiction.
questions.explanation: eka predictions, hydrogen, an anomalous pair, isotope problem.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1913 Moseley measured the frequencies of X-rays emitted by elements and found they were governed by a whole number that increased by one from element to element. This led to a revision of the periodic law.

(i) What is this whole number called?
(ii) State the Modern Periodic Law.
(iii) How does this law resolve the Ar/K anomaly?
(iv) How does it explain the position of isotopes?
questions.answer:
(i) The whole number is the ATOMIC NUMBER (the number of protons).
(ii) Modern Periodic Law: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
(iii) Ordering by atomic number gives argon Z = 18 before potassium Z = 19 automatically, so the chemically correct order matches the numerical order and the anomaly disappears.
(iv) Isotopes have the same atomic number (same number of protons), so they all occupy the SAME position in the table — the isotope problem is removed.
questions.explanation: Atomic number, modern law, Ar/K resolved, isotopes share position.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Modern Periodic Table arranges all elements by increasing atomic number into 7 horizontal rows and 18 vertical columns, further divided into blocks according to the sub-shell being filled.

(i) What are the rows and columns called, and how many of each are there?
(ii) What does the period number tell you about an atom?
(iii) Why do elements in the same group have similar properties?
(iv) Name the four blocks.
questions.answer:
(i) Rows are PERIODS (7 of them) and columns are GROUPS (18 of them).
(ii) The period number equals the number of OCCUPIED electron shells in the atom.
(iii) Because elements in the same group have the SAME number of valence electrons, and chemical behaviour is governed by valence electrons, they show similar properties.
(iv) The four blocks are the s-block, p-block, d-block and f-block.
questions.explanation: 7 periods/18 groups, period = shells, same valence electrons, four blocks.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The position of an element in the periodic table follows from its electronic configuration. Consider an element X with electronic configuration 2, 8, 8, 2.

(i) How many shells are occupied, and what is the period of X?
(ii) How many valence electrons does X have, and what is its group type?
(iii) Identify the element X.
(iv) What is the valency of X?
questions.answer:
(i) Four shells are occupied (2, 8, 8, 2), so X is in PERIOD 4.
(ii) The outermost shell has 2 valence electrons, so X is in GROUP 2 (the alkaline earth metals).
(iii) Total electrons = 2+8+8+2 = 20, so Z = 20; the element is CALCIUM (Ca).
(iv) With 2 valence electrons (≤ 4), the valency is 2.
questions.explanation: 4 shells->period 4; 2 valence e->group 2; Z=20 Ca; valency 2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The elements of period 3 are Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar. As we move from sodium toward argon, several properties change in a regular way.

(i) How does atomic size change from Na to Cl, and why?
(ii) How does metallic character change across this period?
(iii) Which of these elements is the most electronegative (excluding Ar)?
(iv) How does the number of valence electrons change across the period?
questions.answer:
(i) Atomic size DECREASES from Na to Cl. Electrons are added to the same (third) shell while the nuclear charge increases, so the stronger nuclear pull contracts the atom.
(ii) Metallic character DECREASES across the period — the left-hand elements (Na, Mg) are metals, while the right-hand elements (S, Cl) are non-metals.
(iii) Chlorine (Cl) is the most electronegative of these (argon, a noble gas, is excluded).
(iv) The number of valence electrons INCREASES by one at each step, from 1 in Na to 7 in Cl (and 8 in Ar).
questions.explanation: Size decreases, metallic decreases, Cl most electronegative, valence electrons rise.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The alkali metals lithium, sodium and potassium all lie in group 1 of the periodic table, one below the other.

(i) How does atomic size change from Li to K, and why?
(ii) How does metallic character (reactivity) change down this group?
(iii) Why do all three have the same valency?
(iv) Which of the three holds its valence electron most tightly?
questions.answer:
(i) Atomic size INCREASES from Li to K because each successive element has one more electron shell, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus.
(ii) Metallic character (reactivity) INCREASES down the group — K is more reactive than Na, which is more reactive than Li — because larger atoms lose their outer electron more easily.
(iii) All three have ONE valence electron, and valency is set by the number of valence electrons, so each has valency 1.
(iv) LITHIUM holds its valence electron most tightly, because it is the smallest atom and its outer electron is closest to the nucleus.
questions.explanation: Size up, reactivity up, valency 1 for all, Li holds electron tightest.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The halogens fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine form group 17. They react by gaining one electron to complete their outer shell. Their reactivity changes steadily down the group.

(i) How does electronegativity change from F to I, and why?
(ii) Which halogen is the most reactive non-metal?
(iii) How does atomic size change down the group?
(iv) Why does the reactivity of halogens DECREASE down the group?
questions.answer:
(i) Electronegativity DECREASES from F to I, because each step adds a new shell, so the incoming bonding electron is attracted by a nucleus that is farther away and more shielded.
(ii) FLUORINE is the most reactive non-metal — it is the smallest and most electronegative, so it attracts and gains an electron most strongly.
(iii) Atomic size INCREASES down the group, as new shells are added from F to Cl to Br to I.
(iv) Halogens react by GAINING an electron; down the group the atom gets larger and the nucleus's pull on an incoming electron weakens, so it is harder to attract and capture an extra electron. Hence reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine.
questions.explanation: Electronegativity down, F most reactive, size up, weaker pull -> less reactive.
